simple: a part that turns one kind of physical thing (heat, light, pressure, movement) into another, usually an electrical signal.
analogy: the cold-room thermometer, which turns warmth into a needle position.
precise: a device that converts energy or a physical quantity from one form to another; a sensor uses a transducer to produce an electrical quantity (voltage, current, resistance or charge) that depends on the measured quantity.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the circuit that makes a sensor's signal the right size and cleanliness for the converter.
analogy: wiping the thermometer's glass and turning it so the needle can be read from the doorway.
precise: amplification, level shifting, filtering and buffering applied between a transducer and an ADC so that the signal fits the converter's input range and bandwidth.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that turns a voltage into a whole number.
analogy: Amara reading the needle and writing the nearest whole degree.
precise: a circuit that compares an input voltage with a reference and outputs an n-bit code; an ideal n-bit ADC divides its input range into 2^n equal steps. Introduced in F1-08 as part of sampling and quantisation.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the voltage the ADC treats as "full scale".
analogy: the top mark on the thermometer's dial.
precise: the voltage against which an ADC compares its input; for an ideal unipolar n-bit converter, code = floor(Vin / Vref × 2^n), clamped to 0 … 2^n − 1.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); R1 of F1-64 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the voltage difference between two neighbouring codes.
analogy: the gap between two marks on the dial.
precise: Vref / 2^n for an ideal n-bit converter; also called the resolution in volts.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); R1 of F1-64 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small difference between the true voltage and the voltage the code stands for.
analogy: the part of a degree Amara cannot write down.
precise: the difference between the input and the value represented by its code; for an ideal converter reported at mid-step it is at most half an LSB in magnitude.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); R1 of F1-64 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many readings are taken per second.
analogy: how often Amara walks to the cold room.
precise: the number of samples per second, in hertz (Hz); the sample period is Ts = 1 / fs.
source: D2 of F1-64 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: half the sample rate: the fastest wobble the readings can show correctly.
analogy: if Amara reads every half hour, she cannot see anything that swings faster than once an hour.
precise: fs / 2; a band-limited signal whose frequencies are all below it can be reconstructed from its samples (the sampling theorem), and components above it fold back to lower frequencies.
source: D2 of F1-64 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fast wobble that looks like a slow one because it was read too rarely.
analogy: the slow wave in Amara's log book that was never in the cold room.
precise: after sampling at fs, a sinusoid at f is indistinguishable from one at |f − k·fs| for any integer k; the alias seen is the one in 0 … fs/2.
source: D2 of F1-64 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing"); R2 of F1-64 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a filter in front of the ADC that removes wobbles too fast to be sampled.
analogy: a thick case around the thermometer that makes the needle too slow to follow the quick swings.
precise: an analog low-pass filter placed before sampling that attenuates components above the Nyquist frequency enough that their aliases are negligible.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D2 of F1-64 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a circuit that freezes the voltage for a moment so the ADC can measure it.
analogy: Amara taking a photo of the needle so she can read it calmly.
precise: a switch and capacitor that track the input and then hold its value constant during the conversion.
source: D1 of F1-64 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small chip that feels tilting, pushing and turning.
analogy: Lucía's wrist and her sense of turning while she carries the soup.
precise: a sensor package that measures specific force with accelerometers and angular rate with gyroscopes, usually along three perpendicular axes each; a magnetometer is often added. (The F9 courses use the registered analogy "the balance sense in your inner ear", analogy registry.)
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor that feels pushes, and also feels gravity pulling down.
analogy: the weight of the bowl shifting in Lucía's wrist.
precise: a sensor whose output is the specific force along its axis: acceleration minus gravitational acceleration, so at rest it reads 1 g directed opposite to gravity (upwards).
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what an accelerometer really feels: every push except gravity's own pull.
analogy: the table pushing up on the bowl when it rests.
precise: the non-gravitational force per unit mass, f = a − g (vectors), in m/s² or in units of g.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor that measures how fast it is turning.
analogy: Lucía feeling herself turn the corner.
precise: a sensor whose output is the angular rate about its axis, in degrees or radians per second; MEMS gyros used in IMUs measure rate, not angle.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a compass sensor: it measures the magnetic field around it.
analogy: seeing the sunlit courtyard and knowing which way you face.
precise: a sensor that measures the local magnetic field vector; heading can be estimated from its horizontal components once tilt is known, and nearby iron and electric currents disturb it.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor's reading when the true value is zero.
analogy: a kitchen scale that shows 3 grams with nothing on it.
precise: a constant or slowly varying offset added to a sensor's output; it is estimated (calibrated) and subtracted.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the angle error that keeps growing when you add up turning rates.
analogy: after spinning slowly for a long time, Lucía no longer knows which way she faces.
precise: the growth of error in an angle obtained by integrating rate measurements; a constant bias b produces an error b·t that grows linearly with time, and noise adds a random walk.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); R2 of F1-65 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the largest value the sensor can report before it saturates.
analogy: the highest mark on the scale's dial.
precise: the configured measurement range (for example ±4 g); with a 16-bit signed output, one count is range / 32768.
source: D4 of F1-65 (The datasheet of the IMU chosen for the course kit); R1 of F1-65 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a calculation that tells how much of each frequency a list of samples contains.
analogy: sorting the kitchen's noise into the hum of the fridge, the whirr of the mixer and the clatter of plates.
precise: for N samples x[n], X[k] = Σ x[n]·e^−i2πkn/N, k = 0 … N−1; bin k corresponds to k·fs/N hertz; the FFT is a fast algorithm that computes the same values.
source: D2 of F1-65 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a chart of "how big is each frequency" in a signal.
analogy: a list of each kitchen machine and how loud it is.
precise: for a real signal, A[k] = 2|X[k]|/N for 0 < k < N/2 gives the amplitude of a sinusoid at bin frequency k·fs/N.
source: D2 of F1-65 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing"); R4 of F1-65 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor that gives a pulse for every small step a shaft turns.
analogy: the click of the pasta crank at every notch.
precise: a rotary sensor that outputs pulses as the shaft moves; position is known only relative to where counting started. The robotics courses define Encoder for counting wheel turns (RB101).
source: D1 of F1-66 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two pulse signals a quarter of a step apart, so their order tells the direction.
analogy: the second spring set a little behind the first.
precise: two square waves A and B, 90 electrical degrees out of phase; each cycle passes through four states (00, 01, 11, 10 in one direction), and the order of the states gives the direction.
source: D1 of F1-66 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Counts per revolution (CPR) and x4 decoding

term: Counts per revolution (CPR) and x4 decoding
simple: how many counts one full turn gives.
analogy: twenty clicks per turn of the crank.
precise: an encoder with L lines (pulses per channel per revolution) gives 4L counts per revolution when every edge of both channels is counted (x4 decoding), 2L or L with x2 or x1 decoding. Whether a datasheet quotes lines or counts must be checked.
source: D1 of F1-66 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D2 of F1-66 (The datasheet of the encoder or gearmotor-with-encoder chosen for the course kit) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one extra pulse once per turn, to find a known position.
analogy: a painted mark on the crank wheel.
precise: a third channel (often called Z or I) that pulses once per revolution and is used to reset or check the count at a reference angle.
source: D1 of F1-66 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Counts per revolution (CPR) and x4 decoding

simple: a sensor that tells the exact angle at any moment, even just after power-on.
analogy: a crank wheel with the angle printed at every notch.
precise: a rotary sensor that outputs a code for the current angle; optical ones often use a Gray code so that only one bit changes between neighbouring positions.
source: D1 of F1-66 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F1-66 (David Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way of numbering in which the next number always differs in exactly one bit.
analogy: a row of switches where you only ever flip one at a time to count.
precise: a binary code in which successive values differ in one bit; binary b converts to Gray g = b XOR (b >> 1).
source: D4 of F1-66 (David Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: working out how far you went by counting wheel turns.
analogy: Ravi measuring dough by counting clicks.
precise: estimation of displacement from wheel or joint rotation measurements; for a wheel of radius r, distance = 2πr × counts / CPR, valid only while the wheel does not slip.
source: D3 of F1-66 (Kevin M. Lynch, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: measuring distance by timing how long a signal takes to go out and come back.
analogy: Kwame's clap and its echo in the cellar.
precise: a ranging method in which range d = v·t/2, where t is the round-trip time and v the propagation speed; for light in vacuum v = c.
source: D1 of F1-67 (Sebastian Thrun, "Probabilistic Robotics"); D2 of F1-67 (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM), "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor that measures distances with laser light, often in many directions.
analogy: clapping into the dark in every direction, one after another, and timing each echo.
precise: light detection and ranging: an active sensor that emits light (usually laser pulses or modulated light) and measures range from the returned light; a scanning LiDAR sweeps the beam to produce many (angle, range) measurements.
source: D1 of F1-67 (Sebastian Thrun, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one sweep of measurements, and the dots they make when drawn in space.
analogy: a sketch of the storeroom made only from echo times in each direction.
precise: a scan is a set of (bearing, range) readings from one sweep; converting each to Cartesian coordinates (x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ in the sensor frame) gives a 2D point set, or a 3D point cloud for multi-beam sensors.
source: D1 of F1-67 (Sebastian Thrun, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the furthest the sensor can measure, and the special value it reports when no echo came back.
analogy: clapping into an open field: no echo at all.
precise: beyond its maximum range, or when the surface returns too little light, a range sensor reports no valid measurement; drivers encode this as a special value (zero, the maximum, infinity, or a flag) defined in the sensor's documentation.
source: D1 of F1-67 (Sebastian Thrun, "Probabilistic Robotics"); D4 of F1-67 (The datasheet and driver documentation of the LiDAR or depth camera chosen for the course) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: things hidden behind other things.
analogy: the crate in front of the back wall: the clap's echo comes from the crate, and the wall behind it is not heard.
precise: a range sensor measures only the first surface along each beam; regions behind it produce no measurements (a "shadow" in the point set).
source: D1 of F1-67 (Sebastian Thrun, "Probabilistic Robotics"); R2 of F1-67 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far a point jumps sideways between the left and right camera images.
analogy: the pepper grinder jumping when Ines switches eyes.
precise: for two rectified cameras with focal length f (pixels) and baseline B, a point at depth Z appears shifted by disparity d = f·B/Z pixels, so Z = f·B/d.
source: D3 of F1-67 (Richard Hartley, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a depth camera that projects a known pattern and looks at how it bends over objects.
analogy: shining a striped tablecloth pattern on the counter and seeing the stripes shift over the bowls.
precise: active triangulation: a projector casts a known pattern and a camera at a known offset observes it; depth follows from the pattern's displacement, by the same geometry as stereo.
source: D3 of F1-67 (Richard Hartley, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the simplest description of a camera: every ray of light goes through one point and hits a flat image.
analogy: the hole in Nadia's shutter and the picture on the wall.
precise: a projection in which a point (X, Y, Z) in the camera frame maps to image coordinates u = fx·X/Z + cx, v = fy·Y/Z + cy; real lenses add distortion that is calibrated separately.
source: D2 of F1-68 (Richard Hartley, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision"); D1 of F1-68 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the numbers that describe one camera's own geometry: how strongly it magnifies and where its centre is in the image.
analogy: how far the wall is from the hole, and where on the wall the hole's straight-ahead line lands.
precise: the focal lengths fx, fy in pixels and the principal point (cx, cy), often written as the calibration matrix K; obtained by calibration.
source: D2 of F1-68 (Richard Hartley, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a chip covered in tiny light meters, one per pixel.
analogy: Farid's squared paper, one square per pixel.
precise: an array of photodiodes that convert light into charge during the exposure; in a CMOS sensor, each pixel has its own readout transistors and rows are read through column circuits and ADCs.
source: D1 of F1-68 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long each pixel collects light, and the most light it can hold.
analogy: how long a bucket stands in the rain, and how much it holds before it overflows.
precise: the exposure (integration) time is the interval during which a pixel accumulates photo-generated charge; the full-well capacity is the maximum charge before the pixel saturates.
source: D1 of F1-68 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the natural randomness of light: even steady light arrives as uneven raindrops.
analogy: two buckets in the same steady rain never collect exactly the same number of drops.
precise: photon arrivals (and the electrons they produce) follow Poisson statistics, so a mean of N electrons has standard deviation √N and signal-to-noise ratio √N.
source: D3 of F1-68 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D5 of F1-68 (Joseph K. Blitzstein, "Introduction to Probability") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: tiny coloured filters over the pixels, so each pixel measures only red, green or blue.
analogy: Farid colouring each square with only one of three crayons, in a fixed pattern.
precise: a mosaic of colour filters over the sensor; the common Bayer pattern repeats a 2 × 2 tile with one red, two green and one blue filter; full colour is estimated by demosaicing.
source: D1 of F1-68 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: guessing the two missing colours at every pixel from its neighbours.
analogy: filling in each square's missing crayons by looking at the squares around it.
precise: interpolation of a full RGB image from a colour-filter-array image; simple methods produce false colours along sharp edges.
source: D1 of F1-68 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications"); R3 of F1-68 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: reading the picture one row after another, or all at once.
analogy: Farid copying the wall row by row, versus taking a photograph of the whole wall at once.
precise: with a rolling shutter, each row's exposure starts and ends a fixed row time after the previous row's, so moving objects are skewed; with a global shutter, all pixels expose during the same interval.
source: D1 of F1-68 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications"); D4 of F1-68 (The datasheet of the camera module or image sensor chosen for the course) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a motor that spins when you connect it to a battery, and spins the other way if you swap the wires.
analogy: the cellar water wheel, turned by water pressure.
precise: a motor whose rotating winding (armature) is fed through brushes and a commutator that reverse the current in each coil as the rotor turns, producing torque in a fixed direction with a permanent-magnet or wound field.
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the voltage a spinning motor makes by itself, which pushes against the supply.
analogy: the turning wheel pushing back on the water.
precise: the electromotive force induced in the windings by rotation, e = Ke·ω, opposing the applied voltage; it is why current falls as the motor speeds up.
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two numbers saying how much push you get per amp, and how much voltage you get per unit of speed.
analogy: how hard the wheel turns per bucket of water, and how hard it pushes back per turn.
precise: torque constant Kt (N·m per A) and back-EMF constant Ke (V per rad/s); in consistent SI units they are numerically equal for an ideal motor.
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the current and push a motor has when it is held still.
analogy: the wheel stopped by sacks while the water roars through.
precise: at zero speed there is no back-EMF, so the current is V/R and the torque Kt·V/R, the largest values on the torque–speed line; the winding then dissipates V²/R as heat.
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); R1 of F1-69 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a graph showing how a motor slows down as you load it more.
analogy: the wheel's speed for each number of sacks.
precise: for a DC motor at fixed voltage, speed falls nearly linearly from the no-load speed to zero at stall torque; mechanical power, torque × speed, peaks near half the stall torque.
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); R1 of F1-69 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a motor with magnets on the spinning part and coils that stay still, switched by electronics instead of brushes.
analogy: a wheel turned by three water jets that a helper opens and closes in turn as the wheel moves.
precise: a permanent-magnet synchronous motor with stator windings (usually three phases) commutated electronically from rotor-position information (Hall sensors, back-EMF sensing, or an encoder).
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: choosing which coils get current, depending on where the magnets are.
analogy: the helper deciding which jet to open by looking at marks on the wheel.
precise: in six-step (trapezoidal) commutation, three Hall sensors spaced 120 electrical degrees apart give six valid 3-bit patterns; each selects one phase driven high, one low and one floating.
source: D1 of F1-69 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); D5 of F1-69 (The datasheet of the BLDC motor or BLDC driver chosen for the course, including its Hall-to-phase commutation table) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small box that turns its arm to the angle you ask for.
analogy: a wheel with a helper who keeps adjusting the valve until a pointer matches the order slip.
precise: a motor, gearbox, position sensor (often a potentiometer) and controller in one housing, commanded by the width of a repeating pulse; the pulse-to-angle mapping and timing are given by its datasheet.
source: D4 of F1-69 (The datasheet of the hobby servo chosen for the course kit) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: switching a supply on and off very fast, so that on average the motor gets a lower voltage.
analogy: Sven flicking the valves open and shut.
precise: a rectangular switching waveform of fixed frequency whose duty cycle D sets the average output voltage D·Vsupply; the load's inductance and inertia average the pulses.
source: D2 of F1-70 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); D1 of F1-70 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: both switches on one side of the bridge on at once, shorting the supply.
analogy: both valves on one side open: the tank empties straight into the drain.
precise: simultaneous conduction of the high-side and low-side switches of one bridge leg, giving a low-resistance path from supply to ground; even brief overlaps waste power and heat the switches, and long ones destroy them.
source: D1 of F1-70 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-70 (The datasheets of the motor-driver IC, MOSFETs and gate driver chosen for the course kit) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a short pause between switching one side off and the other on.
analogy: Olu waiting until one valve is fully shut before opening the other.
precise: a deliberate delay inserted between the turn-off command of one switch in a leg and the turn-on command of the other, longer than the difference between the switches' turn-off and turn-on delays.
source: D3 of F1-70 (The datasheets of the motor-driver IC, MOSFETs and gate driver chosen for the course kit); R4 of F1-70 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a one-way path that lets a motor's current keep flowing gently when the switch opens.
analogy: Olu's bypass loop that stops the water hammer.
precise: a diode placed so that an inductive load's current can continue when its switch turns off, clamping the switch voltage to about the supply plus one diode drop; in a MOSFET bridge, the body diodes or the opposite switch provide this path.
source: D1 of F1-70 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); R3 of F1-70 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much the motor current wobbles up and down with every PWM pulse.
analogy: how much the water flow surges each time a valve flicks.
precise: the peak-to-peak variation of load current within a PWM period; for a period much shorter than L/R it is about V·D(1−D)/(L·fPWM).
source: D2 of F1-70 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); R2 of F1-70 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what the bridge does with the motor current when it is not driving: let it fade, or short the motor to slow it.
analogy: closing all valves (the wheel spins on) or connecting both sides of the wheel together (the wheel's own push-back slows it).
precise: in coast (fast decay) the current returns through the diodes against the supply and decays quickly, and the motor freewheels; in brake (both low or both high switches on) the motor's back-EMF drives current through the short and produces a braking torque.
source: D2 of F1-70 (Austin Hughes, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); D3 of F1-70 (The datasheets of the motor-driver IC, MOSFETs and gate driver chosen for the course kit) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a helper chip that switches the big transistors quickly and safely.
analogy: a strong assistant who turns the stiff valves fast when Sven gives the word.
precise: a circuit that converts logic-level commands into the gate voltages and currents a power MOSFET needs, including a raised supply for high-side switches, often with built-in dead time and fault protection.
source: D1 of F1-70 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-70 (The datasheets of the motor-driver IC, MOSFETs and gate driver chosen for the course kit) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a ready-made board that drives a brushless motor from a speed command.
analogy: a valve-room helper who reads the wheel's marks and works all the valves by herself.
precise: a three-phase bridge, gate drivers and a microcontroller running commutation (F1-69) and speed control; it accepts a command such as a servo-style pulse or a digital protocol defined in its documentation.
source: D4 of F1-70 (The documentation of the ESC chosen for the course) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

term: Cell, series and parallel (S and P)
simple: a battery pack is several cells joined end to end (more volts) and side by side (more capacity).
analogy: stacking tanks on top of each other raises the pressure; putting them side by side holds more water.
precise: in an nSmP pack, n cells in series multiply the voltage by n, and m strings in parallel multiply the capacity by m; energy scales with both.
source: D4 of F1-71 (Thomas B. Reddy (ed.), "Linden's Handbook of Batteries"); R1 of F1-71 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much charge a battery can give, and how much work that can do.
analogy: how many litres the tank holds, and how much those litres can do at the tank's pressure.
precise: capacity in ampere-hours is the charge delivered under stated test conditions; energy in watt-hours is approximately capacity × average voltage. Both are rated by the maker under specific conditions.
source: D4 of F1-71 (Thomas B. Reddy (ed.), "Linden's Handbook of Batteries"); D1 of F1-71 (The battery maker's datasheet and safety instructions for the pack chosen for the course kit) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Cell, series and parallel (S and P)

simple: a way to say how fast you charge or discharge, compared with the battery's size.
analogy: "1C" empties the tank in about an hour; "2C" in about half an hour.
precise: current divided by the rated capacity in Ah (per hour); the maker states maximum continuous and burst discharge C-rates and the maximum charge rate.
source: D1 of F1-71 (The battery maker's datasheet and safety instructions for the pack chosen for the course kit); D4 of F1-71 (Thomas B. Reddy (ed.), "Linden's Handbook of Batteries") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a battery's voltage drops when you take a lot of current, because the battery itself resists it.
analogy: the narrow tank outlet: the faster the flow, the more pressure is lost there.
precise: to first order, terminal voltage = open-circuit voltage − I·Rint; Rint varies with temperature, state of charge and age, and the drop also heats the cell (I²Rint).
source: D4 of F1-71 (Thomas B. Reddy (ed.), "Linden's Handbook of Batteries"); D3 of F1-71 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: State of charge and cutoff voltage

term: State of charge and cutoff voltage
simple: how full the battery is, and the voltage at which you must stop using it.
analogy: the tank's level gauge, and the mark below which the pump must stop.
precise: state of charge (SoC) is the remaining fraction of capacity; the open-circuit voltage depends on it in a chemistry-specific way; the discharge cutoff is the minimum voltage the maker allows, below which the cell is damaged.
source: D1 of F1-71 (The battery maker's datasheet and safety instructions for the pack chosen for the course kit); D4 of F1-71 (Thomas B. Reddy (ed.), "Linden's Handbook of Batteries") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of everything that uses power, how much, and for how long.
analogy: a list of every tap, machine and toilet in the restaurant with how much water each uses per hour.
precise: a table of loads with their average and peak currents (or powers) at each supply rail, summed to size the battery, regulators, wiring and fuses, with an explicit margin.
source: D3 of F1-71 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: State of charge and cutoff voltage

simple: the supply voltage dips too low for the electronics, so they reset or misbehave.
analogy: the coffee machine shutting down when the pressure drops.
precise: a supply voltage below a device's minimum operating level; microcontrollers usually include a brown-out detector that holds or puts the chip in reset below a configured threshold, given in its datasheet.
source: D5 of F1-71 (The datasheet and reference manual of the course microcontroller); R3 of F1-71 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: starting a motor gently instead of all at once.
analogy: Hamid opening the dishwasher's valve slowly.
precise: ramping a motor's command (or a supply's output) over a set time to limit the inrush current and the resulting voltage drop.
source: R4 of F1-71 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0); D3 of F1-71 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how big the thing you want to measure is compared with the wobble on top of it.
analogy: the soup level compared with the sloshing.
precise: the ratio of signal power to noise power, often given in decibels as 10·log10(Ps/Pn), or as a ratio of amplitudes (20·log10).
source: D1 of F1-72 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: taking many readings and using their average makes random wobble smaller, but slowly.
analogy: Kenji's several dipstick readings.
precise: the mean of N independent readings, each with standard deviation σ, has standard deviation σ/√N; averaging does not reduce offsets or noise that is correlated between readings.
source: D4 of F1-72 (Joseph K. Blitzstein, "Introduction to Probability"); R1 of F1-72 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a calculation that keeps slow changes and smooths away fast wobbles.
analogy: Kenji writing down a value that only moves a tenth of the way towards each new reading.
precise: the first-order recursive filter y[n] = y[n−1] + a·(x[n] − y[n−1]), 0 < a ≤ 1; its gain falls with frequency, and it delays the signal.
source: D3 of F1-72 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing"); R2 of F1-72 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the frequency at which a filter starts to cut a signal noticeably.
analogy: how quickly the soup can really change before Kenji's slow log starts missing it.
precise: the frequency at which the filter's amplitude gain is 1/√2 (−3 dB) of its pass-band gain.
source: D3 of F1-72 (Alan V. Oppenheim, "Discrete-Time Signal Processing") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when two circuits share a wire, the current of one changes the voltage the other sees.
analogy: the shared drain pipe backing up under the soup pot.
precise: interference caused by a current I1 flowing through an impedance Z also in circuit 2's path, adding I1·Z to circuit 2's signal; common in ground returns shared by motors and sensors.
source: D2 of F1-72 (Henry W. Ott, "Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering"); D1 of F1-72 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every part gets its own ground wire back to one common point.
analogy: every drain gets its own pipe to the main sewer.
precise: a grounding layout in which separate return paths meet at a single point, so that one circuit's return current does not flow through another's reference; at high frequency, ground planes and short return loops matter more.
source: D2 of F1-72 (Henry W. Ott, "Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small capacitor next to a chip that supplies quick bursts of current so the supply voltage stays steady.
analogy: a small bucket of water beside each sink for sudden needs.
precise: a capacitor placed close to a device's supply pins, providing a low-impedance local source for fast current changes and keeping supply noise from spreading; values and placement are in the device's datasheet.
source: D1 of F1-72 (Paul Horowitz, "The Art of Electronics"); D5 of F1-72 (The datasheets of the sensor board's sensors and of the microcontroller's ADC chosen for the course) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: ways of running wires so that other wires and motors disturb them less.
analogy: covering a pipe and keeping its supply and return pipes side by side.
precise: twisting a signal and its return wire together keeps the loop area small and cancels much magnetic pickup; a shield (a conductive cover) intercepts electric-field coupling and must be connected at the end the design specifies.
source: D2 of F1-72 (Henry W. Ott, "Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
